column4: Hud asks Aad why they build a sign on every height in play, directly staging Iram's passion for erecting conspicuous markers.
Aad take monumental structures as though they might remain forever, making explicit the permanence fantasy carried by the section's tall buildings.
The heavens are raised بغير عمد ترونها, using the section's عماد root while contrasting divine elevation with human height that needs visible supports.
This second no-pillars formulation joins heaven raised بغير عمد ترونها to mountains cast into earth, bringing both divine supports in the section together.
Aad's boast “who is stronger than us?” is answered inside the ayah by the greater strength of the God who created them.
Hud reminds Aad that God increased them in bodily stature, joining their exceptional height and strength to gifted creation rather than self-made greatness.
The people of Hijr carve houses from mountains while feeling secure, exactly matching the section's delicate opening of massive hard rock.
Salih recalls Thamud building palaces on plains and carving mountains into houses, the fullest parallel to the valley's rock-cut architecture.
Thamud carve houses from mountains with confident skill, foregrounding the same union of precise craft and hard material.
Pharaoh orders Haman to fire clay and build a tower so that he may look toward Moses' God, the section's other human bid for height.
Pharaoh again commands Haman to build him a lofty tower, directly repeating the ruler's vertical construction project.
The tower sought in 40:36 is meant to reach the routes of the heavens and inspect Moses' God; this ayah supplies the project's arrogant upward aim.
Pharaoh is again named ذو الأوتاد, confirming that the “owner of stakes” is a recurring Quranic identity rather than a local phrase in surah 89.
Mountains are made as pegs, setting God's earth-stabilizing أوتادا opposite Pharaoh's claimed stakes.
At the divine disclosure the mountain is made دكا and Moses falls unconscious, directly enacting the section's named root as height becomes level ground.
Dhul-Qarnayn says that when God's promise comes, even the formidable barrier will be made دكاء, so constructed security lasts only by divine leave.
Earth and mountains are lifted and crushed دكة واحدة, a direct Quranic counterpart to the repeated leveling in 89:21.
After 20:105 asks about the mountains, this ayah says God leaves their place a level قاعا صفصفا, the very flat-field image developed in the section.
The plain of 20:106 has neither crookedness nor rise, specifying what remains when every separate height has disappeared.
Thamud's end is expressed by God's crushing them and فسواها, giving the rock-carving people a finale of leveling.
God comes at a building from its foundations and its roof falls upon its makers, precisely showing that when support fails the height above it goes too.
Solomon's body remains upright only through his staff; when it is eaten he falls, a compact scene of a load-bearing support removed.
Ruined towns lie collapsed upon their roofs beside an abandoned well and a lofty palace, gathering built height and its desolation in one landscape.
Aad's wind destroys everything by its Lord's command until only their dwellings can be seen, turning an unmatched civilization into nearly erased traces.
Aad lie like hollow palm trunks, so the section's upright column-like bodies appear felled and emptied on the ground.
The wind uproots people as though they were torn-up palm trunks, another direct reversal from vertical strength to prostrate timber.
God creates everything and determines it with exact measure, joining خلق to تقدير just as the section's craft definition joins making to measuring before cutting.
“Everything We created by measure” gives the section's craft sense of خلق a concise cosmic formulation.
God creates and proportionally shapes, making formation itself an act of fitting rather than the boast of an unprecedented human city.
Following creation and proportion in 87:2, God determines and guides, completing the section's link between making and measure.
God raises the sky and sets the balance, joining height to true measure in the same sentence.
The raised sky and balance of 55:7 lead to the command not to transgress in measure, defining طغيان as crossing a set limit.
The challenge “are you harder to create, or heaven?” answers human claims of singular strength with the heaven God built.
God raises heaven's canopy and proportions it, uniting elevated construction with measured fitting.
The Creator of heavens and earth is able to create the like of human beings, placing خلق and مثل together against any finite claim to be unmatched.
A second challenge asks whether the Creator of heavens and earth can create their like, again joining the section's two key words خلق and مثل.
God is the unprecedented originator of heavens and earth, relocating true production without a prior model from a celebrated city to divine creation.
God is again named the originator of heavens and earth, marking the boundary between created marvels and the One who initiates creation.
The creation of heavens and earth is greater than the creation of humankind, explicitly rescaling human greatness beneath cosmic creation.
God says He built heaven with power, answering Aad's boast of strength through an incomparably larger construction.
The boast in 41:15 ends in a furious wind and a humiliating punishment, turning self-declared height into abasement.
A violent, relentless wind is sent against Aad, beginning the action that uproots their column-like bodies in 54:20.
Aad's destroying wind is introduced as the barren wind sent against them, opening another version of the city's undoing.
The wind of 51:41 leaves whatever it reaches like something decayed, converting apparent solidity into ruined matter.
Aad are destroyed by a furious, violent wind; the following ayah supplies the felled-trunk tableau used by the section.
After the hollow trunks of 69:7, the question whether any remnant remains completes the section's “erased trace” sense.
The rock-carving Thamud end جاثمين in their own homes, brought from confident construction to bodies collapsed against the ground.
The blast seizes Thamud and they lie جاثمين in their dwellings, repeating the fall from secure rock houses to immobility.
Thamud appear as though they had never flourished in those dwellings, directly realizing the section's image of a vanished built trace.
The blast catches the secure mountain-carvers in the morning, showing how abruptly the confidence of 15:82 fails.
What Thamud had acquired avails them nothing after 15:82-83, denying saving power to their skilled rock architecture.
Thamud's houses stand desolate because of their wrongdoing, a direct Quranic view of the built city after its builders are gone.
Thamud receive عذاب الهون after choosing blindness, joining the section's هوان root to the abasement of this very monumental people.
With 51:44 identifying Thamud, this ayah says they could neither stand up nor help themselves, sharply reversing their stone-cutting strength.
Thamud are reduced by one blast to dry fragments like a pen-builder's shattered brushwood, hard rock craft ending as brittle debris.
Thamud are destroyed by الطاغية, turning the section's root of overstepping into the overwhelming force that brings them down.
Pharaoh exalts himself in the land, making moral overreach spatial through علا في الأرض exactly as the section explains upward transgression.
Moses is sent to Pharaoh because he طغى, directly naming the ruler's act as crossing the limit.
Moses and Aaron are jointly sent to Pharaoh with the repeated diagnosis إنه طغى.
The command to approach Pharaoh again gives his defining offense as طغى, preparing his later claim to supreme height.
Pharaoh declares himself “your highest lord,” converting political height into the ultimate claim of elevation.
God seizes Pharaoh for exemplary punishment immediately after the claim in 79:24, supplying the forced descent that answers it.
Pharaoh is described as high in the land and one of the extravagant, explicitly coupling elevation with exceeding bounds.
Pharaoh and his chiefs act arrogantly toward Moses and Aaron and are called a lofty people, another formulation of height as rebellion.
Pharaoh is described as عاليا among the transgressors, putting height and limit-breaking side by side in his own characterization.
Pharaoh and his forces act arrogantly in the land and suppose they will not return, joining elevation to the illusion of permanence.
God seizes Pharaoh and his forces and casts them into the sea, the downward answer to the arrogance of 28:39 and tower of 28:38.
God destroys what Pharaoh and his people manufactured and what they had raised, directly extending the ruler's fall to his constructions.
The final home is assigned to those who seek neither elevation nor corruption in the land, exactly reversing 89:11-12 and Pharaoh's علا.
When the water طغى it rises beyond its boundary, supplying the physical overflowing sense behind the section's moral account of transgression.
Mountains are removed, the earth is left bare and all people are gathered, staging the open judgment ground after vertical landmarks vanish.
Humanity is presented before the Lord صفا on the bare ground of 18:47, matching the section's row-like plain and judgment rows.
The Spirit and angels stand صفا on the Day, an especially close parallel to the angels arranged row upon row in 89:22.
The angels say “we are indeed the ranged ones,” identifying ordered صف as their own stance.
Those who stand صفا are likened to a compacted building, uniquely joining the section's row and constructed-body images.
The mountains are pulverized completely, a direct nonlexical parallel to the breaking and leveling denoted by دك.
After their pulverizing in 56:5, the mountains become scattered dust, specifying what remains of former mass and height.
Earth and mountains quake and the mountains become a heap of loose sand, replacing stable vertical bodies with collapsing grains.
The mountains are blown away, another concise scene in which the land's dominant heights cease to hold their place.
The mountains are set in motion, removing the fixity that makes structures and landmarks seem permanent.
Mountains become like carded wool, a vivid transformation of the hardest elevated mass into light, separated fibers.
Mountains become like wool, another judgment image of solid height losing both density and shape.
Mountains move away in motion, giving the section's final plain a repeated Quranic setting.
The earth is stretched out flat, directly corresponding to the section's leveled eschatological ground.
The question about the mountains introduces the explicit answer in 20:106-107 that their place will be a perfectly level plain.
The sky is presented for contemplation as something raised, echoing the divine elevation that needs no human column.
The mountains are presented as things set upright, the Quranic verb نصبت closely matching the section's repeated act of erection.
Beside raised sky and erected mountains, the earth is spread out, joining height and level ground within one sequence.
God casts firm mountains into earth lest it sway and makes rivers and roads, explaining what divine earth-pegs do rather than merely how they look.
God provides landmarks and stars for guidance, contrasting useful orientation with Aad's playful markers on every height.
Firm mountains and broad passes are placed on earth so people may be guided, combining anchoring heights with traversable ground.
God anchors the mountains, expressing the fastening action that the section sees in a peg.
The servants of the Merciful walk the earth هونا, making voluntary gentleness and lowliness the answer to tyrants who force themselves upward.
The command not to walk exultantly on earth opposes monumental self-display with an embodied refusal of height.
Moderating one's gait and lowering one's voice shows the chosen form of descent that follows the prohibition of swagger in 31:18.
The human being transgresses, extending the section's account of elevated peoples into a general diagnosis of human behavior.
The cause of 96:6 is seeing oneself self-sufficient, the inner claim beneath both monumental strength and Pharaoh's height.
The answer to human transgression in 96:6-7 is to prostrate and draw near, chosen lowering becoming true approach.
Hearts find طمأنينة in God's remembrance, clarifying the inward rest named by the section's tranquil soul beyond its physical low-ground sense.
A secure, مطمئنة town with abundant provision turns to hunger and fear through ingratitude, uniting city, tranquility, provision and reversal.
God does not expand provision without limit because people would transgress on earth; He sends it by measure, directly linking رزق, measure and طغيان.
One whose provision is constrained is told to spend from what God gave, supplying the faithful response to scarcity instead of “my Lord humiliated me.”
The Prophet is told to say that his Lord expands and constrains provision, while most people do not understand the meaning of either condition.
Wealth and children do not bring a person near to God, directly correcting the honor-by-abundance assumption addressed in 34:36 and surah 89.
True honor with God belongs to the most mindful, setting an explicit measure of كرامة against wealth, stature and construction.
God makes the earth ذلولا and commands people to walk its paths, matching the section's walked, smoothed road and contrasting that lived smoothness with violent leveling.
God makes the earth a spread for people, establishing the habitable ground on which the next ayah's broad paths are walked.
People travel wide pathways through the spread earth of 71:19, a direct Quranic scene for the section's walked, smoothed road.
The command to worship God is itself called a straight path, bringing the عبد root and the road image into explicit relation.
A straight path is named immediately before the protected “My servants” of 15:42, making the section's service-and-road meeting textual.
“My servants” have no satanic authority over them on the straight path named in 15:41, joining destination, service and way.
Every community is told to worship God and avoid الطاغوت, directly opposing عبد to the same root-field of transgressive height.
Those who avoid worshiping الطاغوت and turn to God receive good news as عباد, placing the section's opposed roots within one ayah.
Earlier peoples were stronger, worked the earth and developed it more fully, yet their material achievement did not prevent judgment.
Former peoples were stronger and left greater آثار in the earth, but God seized them, directly answering reliance on monumental traces.
The Quran again points to peoples stronger and more numerous whose acquisitions did not save them, repeating the section's civilizational lesson.
Travelers are asked to see the end of predecessors who were stronger, yet no created strength could frustrate God.
Prosperous towns are destroyed and their dwellings are scarcely inhabited afterward, another scene of built abundance becoming an abandoned trace.
A town lies fallen upon its roofs before God demonstrates restoration, putting ruined construction and renewed creation in the same episode.
Qarun and his house are swallowed into the earth, turning displayed wealth and architectural place into a literal descent below the ground.
Witnesses of Qarun's fall recognize that God expands and constrains provision, joining the swallowed house to the correction of wealth-based honor.
The wealth-counter supposes his property will make him immortal, stating in personal terms the same delusion carried by Aad's enduring monuments.
The عماد root reappears as extended columns enclosing punishment, reversing the column from an emblem of proud support into part of confinement.
“Nothing is like Him” reserves absolute incomparability for God, setting a boundary around the merely relative claim that no city resembled Iram.
No one is comparable to God, again distinguishing divine uniqueness from a created city's unmatched human scale.
Death reaches people even inside lofty fortified towers, directly denying that height and strong building can secure permanence.
The spider's house is the weakest house, supplying the opposite boundary to confidence in columns, rock and monumental shelter.
The good word is a tree with firm root and branch in heaven, offering a vertical form whose lasting height depends on a sound foundation.
The corrupt word is like a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, an organic version of height collapsing when its support is lost.
A fortified people think their strongholds will protect them, but their houses are destroyed, sharply reversing architectural confidence.
A building founded on a crumbling brink collapses with its builder, making moral foundation and structural fall one exact image.
God alone holds heaven and earth from passing away; if they cease, no one else can hold them, contrasting divine sustaining with visible supports.
God holds the sky from falling upon earth except by permission, another direct counterimage to loads borne by human columns.
Mountains that appear fixed pass like clouds, exposing the apparent solidity of even the greatest natural structures as provisional.
The mountains called pegs in 78:7 are set moving and become a mirage, giving the surah itself a creation-to-judgment reversal.
Stones split and release water or fall in awe of God while some hearts are harder, showing hard rock opened and lowered without human carving.
A struck rock releases twelve springs by God's command, setting divine opening of stone beside Thamud's painstaking apertures.
The challenge to become stone or iron if one doubts resurrection turns maximum hardness into no barrier to God's recreating power.
A person is مطمئن only while worldly good lasts and turns away under trial, distinguishing circumstantial ease from the section's truly tranquil soul.
Those satisfied and مطمئن with the nearer life locate their rest in the passing ground, the opposite orientation from return to God.
Creation including mountains bows to God, and one whom God يهن has no one to honor him; chosen prostration and imposed abasement meet here.
God grants and removes dominion, exalts and abases, placing every human rise and fall under the same agency.
A humiliating punishment answers those who acted arrogantly on earth, making هوان the measured reversal of false elevation.
The proud walker can neither split the earth nor reach the mountains in height, fixing a concrete limit on human vertical ambition.
Humanity is created in the best stature, beginning a two-ayah movement from fitted upright form to the lowest condition.
The well-formed human of 95:4 is returned to the lowest of the low, a direct creation-to-lowering reversal.
The coming event is “lowering, raising,” condensing the section's two opposed movements into one description of judgment.
No human before Muhammad was granted immortality, placing an explicit boundary against building as though one could remain forever.
God gives portable dwellings from animal hides, a Quranic tent scene that sets the section's tent-pole sense beside marble permanence.
Solomon's workers make elevated chambers and تماثيل, but the passage commands gratitude, contrasting skilled monumental craft with Aad's boastful use of it.
This ayah names the people of al-Hijr and their rejection of messengers, fixing the حجر place-name and moral identity for the carving scene in 15:82.
Immediately after Aad's monuments, Hud condemns their tyrannical striking, showing that the architecture belongs to a broader posture of coercive power.
Aad's destruction follows the monument and strength speech of 26:128-130, completing that passage's rise-and-fall arc.
After Hud's warning, Aad's last remnant is cut off, reinforcing the section's secondary image of a once-visible trace erased.
The punishment seizes Thamud after their mountain carving in 26:149, supplying that version of the craft's failed security.
Dhul-Qarnayn asks for blocks of iron and fills the gap between two heights, beginning the massive barrier later made دكاء.
Iron is heated and covered with molten copper, specifying the formidable material construction whose promised leveling gives 18:98 its force.
The barrier cannot be scaled or pierced, establishing its apparent impregnability immediately before God promises to level it.
The earth is replaced by another earth when all emerge before God, enlarging the section's leveled judgment ground beyond altered topography.
The heavens nearly rupture, earth splits and mountains collapse, another sequence in which the greatest structures cannot bear a false divine claim.
The trumpet makes creatures fall, then a second blast leaves them standing and looking, a bodily version of the section's standing/fallen opposition.
The oath by those ranged صفا echoes the ordered line that the section hears both in angels and in flat ground.
God creates, proportions and balances the human being, extending the section's measured-craft sense from leather or city to the body.
God composes the human in whatever form He wills, completing the fitted formation described in 82:7.
After raised sky and the ban on transgressing the balance, people are told to establish weight justly and not diminish measure.
God expands and constrains provision while worldly life is only brief enjoyment, placing material plenty and restriction within one larger scale.
God expands provision for some and constrains it for others with full knowledge, separating measured رزق from personal worth.
The person who gathers and repeatedly counts wealth supplies the immediate posture behind the immortality delusion in 104:3.
Qarun goes out before his people in splendor, establishing the displayed height of wealth that is literally swallowed with his house in 28:81.
Pharaoh boasts of Egypt's kingdom and rivers flowing beneath him, another self-presentation of earthly possession as superior height.
Pharaoh and his people are drowned after provoking God, completing the descent from his boast in 43:51.
God makes earth a cradle and threads roads through it, a direct nonlexical parallel to the section's ground made fit for passage.
The repeated cradle-and-roads formula again places traversable ways within a divinely prepared earth.
Jesus says to worship God and calls that the straight path, explicitly pairing service with a road.
Jesus again names worship of the one Lord as a straight path, repeating the meeting between عبد and traversable way.
A third Jesus saying identifies worship of God with the straight path, preserving the same root-image relation in another context.
The section's carving definition uses a garment's جيب as its model aperture; this ayah names those garment openings in an actual clothing scene.
Moses is told to put his hand into his جيب before confronting Pharaoh, placing the section's collar-opening image inside the Pharaoh cycle.
The command to insert the hand into the جيب is repeated in the very surah that also contains Pharaoh's tower, connecting two details developed by the section.
The source dictionary defines دكاء through a camel without a hump; this invitation to contemplate the camel leads directly to raised sky, erected mountains and spread earth.
A burden is removed from the Prophet, beginning a small sequence about load, back and elevation that echoes the section's support vocabulary.
The burden had weighed heavily upon the Prophet's back, furnishing a bodily counterpart to a support bending under load.
After the back's burden is removed, the Prophet's remembrance is raised, completing the sequence's movement from weight to elevation.
On resurrection people hurry as though toward a نصب; if understood as an erected goal-marker, the simile faintly recalls the section's desert stones set up as signs.
